Linoleum is a type of flat, smooth material used to cover floors. Think of it as a tough, thin sheet — almost like a very firm, dense mat — that gets laid down on top of a floor's surface to protect it, make it easier to clean, and make it look nicer.
What it looks like and feels like

Linoleum comes as a large, long roll (similar to how a carpet roll looks) or as flat square tiles. When unrolled or laid flat, it forms a continuous, smooth, even surface. It is firm but has a very slight flexibility to it — it won't crack like ceramic if you bend it gently, but it isn't soft or squishy either. The surface is slightly smooth and can feel a little waxy or matte to the touch. It can be found in a single solid color or printed with patterns — checkerboard patterns, geometric designs, wood-look patterns, and so on.

This is what makes linoleum genuinely interesting: it is made almost entirely from natural materials. The main ingredient is linseed oil (oil that comes from the flax plant), which is allowed to oxidize and thicken into a tough, rubbery solid. This is then combined with materials like powdered cork, wood flour (very fine wood dust), ground limestone, tree resins, and natural pigments for color. All of this gets pressed firmly onto a backing layer — usually a sheet of burlap (a coarse woven fabric) or canvas — which gives it stability and makes it easier to handle and install.

Because it comes from plant-based and mineral sources rather than from plastics or synthetic chemicals, linoleum is considered a relatively natural, eco-friendly material compared to many modern flooring options.

Linoleum is used as flooring — it is installed on the floors of rooms. It has historically been especially popular in:

  • Kitchens and bathrooms, because it resists water and is easy to wipe clean
  • Schools and hospitals, because it is very durable, hygienic, and can handle heavy foot traffic
  • Offices and hallways, for the same durability reasons
  • Living spaces in homes, especially in the mid-20th century when it was extremely common

You can find it glued directly to the floor surface or simply laid down over it.

Linoleum's rise to widespread popularity came down to a few practical advantages:

  1. Durability — it holds up well over many years of daily use.
  2. Easy maintenance — dirt, dust, and spills sit on the surface and can be swept or mopped away easily.
  3. Comfort — it is slightly warmer underfoot compared to bare stone or ceramic tiles, and has just a little give, making it less tiring to stand on for long periods.
  4. Affordability — it was much cheaper than wood, stone, or ceramic tiles.
  5. Versatility — it could be made in many colors and patterns to suit different tastes.
An important distinction: linoleum vs. vinyl flooring

Today, many people use the word "linoleum" loosely to refer to any smooth, sheet-style floor covering — but strictly speaking, this is inaccurate. True linoleum is made from natural materials as described above. Vinyl flooring, on the other hand, is made from PVC plastic (a synthetic, petroleum-derived material) and is a completely different product, even though it can look almost identical to linoleum on the surface. Vinyl became very common from the mid-20th century onward and gradually replaced linoleum in many homes, which is likely why the two get confused so often.

If you pick up a piece of true linoleum and examine its cut edge, you will see that the color goes all the way through the material — it is solid color throughout. Vinyl, by contrast, typically has its pattern only printed on the top surface with a plain backing underneath.

One additional and notable use of linoleum outside of flooring is in printmaking. Artists use blocks of linoleum as a carving surface: they cut a design into the surface using sharp tools, then roll ink over it and press it onto paper to make prints. This technique is called linocut (or linoleum block printing). The material works well for this because it is firm enough to hold sharp, clean carved edges, but soft enough to be cut with hand tools without great effort.

Linoleum is a durable, smooth, flat floor-covering material made from natural ingredients (mainly linseed oil, cork, and wood flour) pressed onto a fabric backing. It is installed on floors in homes, schools, hospitals, and other buildings, valued for being tough, easy to clean, slightly warm and comfortable underfoot, and available in many colors and patterns. It is distinct from vinyl flooring, which looks similar but is made of plastic. It is also used in art as a block for making printed designs.
